narrative:
The model estimated a 72% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a high risk estimate, and it is why your application was denied: the decision reflects predicted bar-exam risk, not a judgment that you cannot succeed.

The strongest factor was your undergraduate GPA of 2.60, which is below the 3.23 average among accepted applicants; this pulled the prediction most strongly toward failure. The second most influential factor was your upper-middle family-income bracket, which nudged the estimate toward failure but was far less decisive; it is also a common bracket among accepted students. The third factor was your first-year class-standing decile of 7, slightly above the accepted average of 6; it leaned toward failure, though only modestly. Your LSAT score of 40 is above the accepted average of 37.18, a positive signal, but it did not outweigh the academic-risk factors the model weighted most heavily.

To strengthen a future application, focus on what you can change. Take additional rigorous coursework to show improved academic performance, ask an admissions counselor about explaining any GPA context, and consider programs that review applicants holistically. Speak with an adviser about whether delaying, retaking the LSAT for an even stronger score, or completing post-baccalaureate work would best demonstrate readiness for law study and bar success.
